newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia stocks seen lacklustre in 2nd half.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia stocks seen lacklustre in 2nd half.

text.p: Malaysian stocks are unlikely to shine in the second half of 1997 after being battered by credit curbs and a slowdown in corporate earnings, analysts and fund managers said on Wednesday.
"The effects of the measures implemented by the central bank would only begin to emerge by the end of the year," said Patrick Tan, assistant director at ABN Amro Hoare Govett in Kuala Lumpur.
"The squeeze on lending will have a braking effect on corporate earnings," he added.
Central Bank Negara Malaysia in March imposed curbs on lending for property and share financing as a pre-emptive measure to prevent a property bubble forming as it had in Thailand.
But foreign currency speculators took the opportunity to sell the ringgit, putting upward pressure on short-term interest rates. Local share prices suffered as a result.

The benchmark Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks stood at a 1997 closing high of 1,270.67 on February 28, just ahead of the release of Bank Negara's 1996 annual report, which contained the new policy measures.
By May 19, the index had plunged 18 percent to close at a year low so far of 1,041.39.
The index was at 1,079.78 at midday on Wednesday with local investors largely ignoring news that Thailand was floating the baht, a move that had shaken some regional stock markets.
The Thai announcement was seen by most local observers as good news for the region, as it removed much uncertainty about Thailand's exchange rate system.
Analysts said the current slump in Malaysian share prices reflected a widespread belief that corporate earnings growth would slow down. But estimates varied on the extent of a slowing.

"People are looking forward to 1998 and 1999. We foresee earnings growth to slow down from 17 percent in 1997 to 14 percent in 1998 and 11 percent in 1999. For 11 percent growth I would not be paying a 16-times price-to-earnings ratio," said the head of research at a foreign brokerage. "There is no reason for people to buy Malaysia at the moment."
Foreign fund managers looking at emerging markets share a similar view. The flow of foreign funds into and out of the Kuala Lumpur stock market has always been a key factor for its direction.
Hugh Young, managing director at Aberdeen Asset Managers in Singapore, said that Malaysian stock prices were on the expensive side compared to those in other emerging markets.
"We have not found much value in Malaysia for some time, as prices are on the dear side. We are finding more and more value in Eastern Europe and even places like Lebanon and Egypt," he added.
But several local fund managers were more optimistic.
Peter Wong Say Fun, vice president of MBf Unit Trust Management, said: "We are quite happy about the market".
"Many people are predicting a fall in earnings growth of one or two percentage points, but at 15-16 percent it's still pretty good," said Wong.
The Malaysian government's budget, to be announced in October, could also have a significant influence on the direction of share prices, said Wong.
"I hope the budget will contain a one- or two-percentage point corporate tax rate cut," said Wong.
Predictions for the level of the Composite Index at year's end ranged from 880 to 1,250.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-206 2323)
